title: Opinion - Trump’s radical plan is to make the postal service an election gatekeeper
description: The potential to interfere with voters' ability to vote by mail is not a bug but a feature of a system designed to restrict a practice that Democrats have used more often than Republicans in recent el...
fullText:
The Trump administration has filed its third emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking to lift a district court injunction that blocked President Trump's U.S. Postal Service regulations imposing strict formatting and data-submission requirements on states' mail-in ballots. A whistleblower has warned that these regulations could cause many ballots to arrive late or not at all ahead of the November midterm elections.

Plaintiffs have argued that these requirements violate the constitutional provisions that restrict election administration to the states and Congress, with no role for the executive. Equally important, and overlooked, is that the administration's scarcely disguised partisan regulations violate a nearly 60-year American tradition of insulating the postal service from politics.

The potential to interfere with voters' ability to vote by mail is not a bug but a feature of a system designed to restrict a practice that Democrats have used more often than Republicans in recent elections.

Trump has made no secret of his longstanding hostility to voting by mail and objective of controlling voting nationally. "Republicans should fight very hard when it comes to statewide mail-in voting," he declared in 2020, because "for whatever reason, [it] doesn't work out well for Republicans." This year, in February, he said, "The Republicans should say, 'We want to take over.' … The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting."

His administration now officially describes its sweeping new postal service restrictions on mail ballots as election-integrity measures, not partisan ones. However, it has provided no proof of the alleged widespread fraud that the regulations would allegedly deter.

The rule doesn't just put occasional errors at risk. It is designed so that a single failure can void an entire jurisdiction's mailing. Even before finalizing the rule, internal postal service officials warned that if even one ballot's barcode in a bulk mailing fails to scan properly during verification, this policy would reject and return the entire batch.

Thus, disrupting an election doesn't require any bad actor at the local level; it only requires ordinary human error, which is guaranteed at scale, colliding with zero tolerance. The regulations would likely upend voting in the eight states where voting is conducted almost entirely by mail, like Washington and Oregon. Seven of these states, with the exception of Utah, lean Democratic.

Washington, which automatically mails ballots to more than 5 million registered voters, says compliance could require destroying and replacing more than 5 million envelopes already printed for November. It would mean fundamentally reworking procedures only weeks before voting begins. The errors that would surely arise in such a rushed process could jeopardize the entire election process of mail-in states.

Similar disruptions would also occur in states like Arizona that rely heavily but not strictly on mail-in voting. In Maricopa County, Ariz., which mails more than 2 million ballots in its initial run, a single misprinted barcode could delay the delivery of every ballot to every voter in the county.

In addition, the Postmaster General has admitted that the U.S. Postal Service will withhold delivery from any state that refuses to hand over its voter manifest. The rule therefore gives partisan opponents of mail-in voting two independent levers, one technical and one administrative, capable of stopping ballots before they reach voters.

The postal apparatus itself embodies a civic lineage older than the Constitution. In 1775, guided by Benjamin Franklin, the first Postmaster General, the Second Continental Congress established the postal service. And as with today's mail-in voting process, the early postal service facilitated democracy.

The mail served as an egalitarian highway of democratic debate, intended to distribute independent newspapers and correspondence without royal or partisan interference. The U.S. Postal Service was designed to serve as a neutral common carrier, not an executive gatekeeper or a roving board of canvassers.

"The country may not even have come into existence but for the postal service," said historian Stephen Allen Kochersperger. Through the material it disseminated, "people were reading, getting ideas of what it would be like to be an independent country."

In the late 20th century, reformers from both parties worried that partisan politics had infected the postal service. With overwhelming bipartisan support, Congress enacted the landmark Postal Reorganization Act of 1970. A central purpose was to insulate the mail from presidential and partisan political control. Upon signing the bill, President Nixon noted that his Democratic and Republican postmasters general agreed on one point: "There is no Republican way or Democratic way to deliver the mail. There is only the right way."

The act converted the postal service into an independent public corporation with a bipartisan Board of Governors — no more than five of the nine members can belong to the same party — and gave that board, not the president, the power to appoint and remove the postmaster general. By asking the Supreme Court to lift the Boston court's injunction, the administration seeks to invert the purpose of the postal service, turning an independent carrier into an instrument of executive election policing for partisan gain.

Benjamin Franklin would be turning in his grave.

Allan J. Lichtman is Distinguished Professor of History at American University, co-host of "Lichtman Live," and author of 15 books, most recently "Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation."

title: Vote against assisted dying 'cruel and inhumane'
description: Terminally ill people in the West Country say they will continue to campaign for assisted dying.
fullText:
A woman living with terminal cancer has called the decision not to legalise assisted dying "unfair, cruel and inhumane".

Nadine Thomas, from Dursley in Gloucestershire, hoped the vote, which went before MPs in Parliament last week, would enable her to choose what to do as her bone cancer progresses and treatment stops working.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed terminally ill people in England and Wales to legally end their own lives. The bill stipulated that any approval would be subject to strict safeguards, but opponents argued they were insufficient.

MPs voted 286 to 270 against it on Friday. It now cannot be reconsidered until at least the next parliament.

Nadine Thomas has campaigned in favour of the bill for the last two years so she and other terminally ill people could be "given the same consideration and dignity" as animals at the end of their lives.

"We're not worried about dying, we know we're going to die. It's how we die - we want to do it with dignity on our own terms - and for me now the chances of that happening are pretty slim," she said.

"We are expected to suffer to our very last dying breath which is unfair, it's cruel, it's inhumane."

Jenny Carruthers, from Bath in Somerset, said the result of the vote was "absolutely crushing".

She previously cared for her partner, who died of cancer in 2013.

Now living with terminal bone cancer herself, Carruthers said she wanted to have the choice to end her life at home on her terms and would continue to campaign for change.

"It's very tiring, physically and emotionally over the whole year and listening to the campaign and constantly being blocked by something that feels very unjust is a hard thing to carry," she said.

"The effect of the illnesses on our bodies just means that its harder, it's physically harder to stand there, it's physically harder to get there and to summon the courage."

The bill was originally voted for by MPs 17 months ago, but it was back in parliament this year after it stalled in the House of Lords.

MPs were given a free vote which meant they did not have to follow party lines.

This time 87 MPs did not vote - including 56 from Labour.

Gideon Amos, the Liberal Democrat MP for Taunton and Wellington, was among those who voted against assisted dying because he believed it would have impacted the freedoms of disabled and vulnerable people.

"I was fundamentally concerned that if people were to be offered assisted dying without the option of proper mental health care or palliative care then that would not be a real choice," he said.

Amos added that he feared dying people would take the option to end their lives "because they feel a burden".

Instead, he said he would like to see more support for hospice and palliative care.

title: If You Love 'The Paper,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
description: Another hilarious comedy set in the world of journalism.
fullText:
The Paper isn’t exactly a sequel to The Office—despite existing in the same universe and sharing the character Oscar Nuñez (played by Office alum Oscar Martinez), the show is its own animal. Unlike Michael Scott, Ned Sampson (Domhnall Gleeson) has a noble quest in saving the Toledo Truth Teller from the sad fate facing most local newspapers, and that shift in focus gives The Paper its own identity. And yet it’s as hilarious as The Office ever was, filled with the same mockumentary-inspired spit-takes and ridiculous capers (largely thanks to Esmeralda, played by Sabrina Impacciatore, who is kind of like Michael and Dwight rolled into one spectacular character).

If you’ve already torn through the show’s first two seasons and you’ve watched all the streamalike shows out there, then the next move is obvious: Watch the 1994 film The Paper.

Although they share a title, there’s no direct connection between the show and the movie—but they’re more similar than you might think. Both are focused on the slow, grinding decline of journalism in America; Ned wants to return the Truth Teller to something resembling a real newspaper, and metro editor Henry Hackett (Michael Keaton) wants to save The New York Sun from (you guessed it) steep budget cuts and an ownership more interested in monetizing its assets than great journalism.

1994’s The Paper, directed by Ron Howard and co-written by David Koepp and his brother Stephen (then an editor at Time Magazine), has a very different style of comedy from The Paper’s mockumentary approach—it’s rougher, edgier, and comes from the fast-paced, motor-mouthed screwball comedy tradition. But it’s just as funny, from the swirl of overheard conversations in the busy newsroom (this is a film that rewards multiple viewings to catch all the little jokes) to the way Keaton’s performance edges closer and closer to Beetlejuice territory as the pressure on Henry mounts (seriously, by the end of the infamous phone-call scene, he’s basically channeling the undead bio-exorcist).

If you’re looking for a comedy like the Peacock show, one that celebrates both journalism and the human beings who think it matters, you’ll definitely love this movie. Plus, it’s got a stacked cast: Aside from Keaton operating at his absolute peak, you’ve got Glenn Close, Robert Duvall, and Marisa Tomei, and Jason Alexander and Catherine O’Hara in small but memorable roles. And if the sort of big tabloid newspaper like The New York Sun is almost extinct these days, that’s part of what makes the movie so effective—just like the series, it starts with the assumption that these papers and the people who work at them matter, and are worth celebrating. Rent The Paper on Prime Video.

Need more journalistic levity than The Paper (and The Paper) can provide? Read on for more movie suggestions that fans of the show will love.

A massive critical and box-office hit in 1987, James L. Brooks' Broadcast News is more of a dramedy than a straightforward comedy—though it has many hilarious moments, including the scene where aspiring news anchor Aaron (Albert Brooks) can’t stop sweating during his big chance on camera. Holly Hunter plays a sharp producer torn between her journalistic ethics and her attraction to a slick but not particularly bright (or ethical) new anchor, played by a hilariously befuddled William Hurt. Its journalistic setting and its concerns over an institution being destroyed by corporate interests and abandoned principles will resonate with fans of The Paper—and it’s a terrific movie in general. Rent Broadcast News on Prime Video.

Want another comedy set in the offices of a struggling newspaper? Check out this forgotten classic from director Joan Micklin Silver (Crossing Delancey). In the mid-1970s, The Back Bay Mainline is a local alternative newspaper struggling to transition from its activist origins to a more mature business. The offices are shabby, the staff underpaid (a truly funny Jeff Goldblum plays music critic Max Arloft, who notes at one point that he takes home $75 a week, which would be about $11k per year in 2026 money), and the question of whether their revolutionary days actually achieved anything hangs in the air as a corporate takeover looms on the horizon. The humor is more subtle and the gender politics are, well, what you might expect from 1976—but there’s charm to spare. Stream Between the Lines on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want fast-paced, crackling humor with a newspaper backdrop, this all-timer is a must-watch. When newspaper editor Walter Burns (Cary Grant in Ultra Cary Grant Mode) discovers his best reporter (and ex-wife), Hildy (Rosalind Russell), is not only getting married but also leaving her career, he decides to win her back and keep her at the paper. He asks her to cover one last story while doing everything he can to ruin her new relationship and convince her that she’s meant to be a reporter—and with him. The dialogue is incredibly fast, very funny, and any fan of The Paper will love it. Stream His Gal Friday on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Fubo, or rent it on Prime Video.

This sweet, funny romantic comedy follows Becky Fuller (Rachel McAdams), who accepts a job as producer at struggling morning show DayBreak. Finding the production in chaos, she uses contractual magic to force veteran newscaster Mike Pomeroy (a crusty Harrison Ford) to become the show’s co-host alongside Colleen Peck (Diane Keaton), to his horror. The battle of wills between Becky and Mike, the battle to save the show, and Becky’s struggle to be taken seriously by the men around her (including her love interest, fellow producer Adam (Patrick Wilson), are packed with sharp jokes and observations about the modern age of news and media—perfect for fans of The Paper. Stream Morning Glory on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Any time fans of a mockumentary-style comedy go looking for a movie, they will eventually find their way to one of Christopher Guest’s classic entries. For fans of The Paper, the best choice from that list is Best in Show. Co-written with Schitt’s Creek’s Eugene Levy, the setting (a national dog show) couldn’t be further from a tiny Midwest newspaper, but the vibe and joke structures are the same, with “talking head” interviews delivering plenty of belly laughs from folks who are so deep in the sauce of their subculture they don’t see how bizarre it looks to outsiders—but, just like Ned’s belief in the power of journalism, underneath all the jokes is a sweet sincerity. If your favorite part about The Paper is the documentary conceit, check this one out. Stream Best in Show on The Roku Channel, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

title: How Bone Conduction Headphones Work (and When You Should Use Them)
description: They really do send sound through your bones. And yes, they're safe.
fullText:
I love my bone conduction headphones. I wear them when I’m running so that I can hear traffic approaching. I also love them for noisy environments where I need to put in earplugs—since the headphones don’t require my ear canal to be open, I can use earplugs and still be able to hear my bone-conducted music. But there's no denying that bone conduction headphones offer a rather different experience than traditional earbuds. What’s going on with this strange technology, and what are the downsides? I’ll explain.

Normally, when we hear a sound from something around us, the sound waves travel through air until they hit our eardrum, located inside the ear canal. The eardrum vibrates in time with the music—really, the frequency of the sound—and transmits that vibration to tiny bones located in what’s called our middle ear.

That's the only part of hearing that you'll need to understand for this explainer. But if you're curious, after the vibrations get to those little bones, they are then transmitted to the inner ear. There, in the cochlea, the sound waves are translated into signals sent to our brain and then further processed into our perception of sound. All of that is outside the scope of this article, though. We’re just interested in how the vibrations get from our headphones to the middle ear.

There’s another way to vibrate those middle ear bones, though: you can do it directly, by sending vibrations right through the head. According to legend, Beethoven would bite his conducting wand and hold it against his piano, so that he could “hear” through his teeth. You can try this right now, with any old earbuds: turn on some music and hold your earbud’s speaker against your tooth. You’ll hear the music. Wild, huh? You can even buy novelty lollipops that play music through your teeth—bite down on the candy and you'll hear a song.

We actually hear bone-conducted sounds all the time. Every time you speak, you’re hearing your own voice through bone (and soft tissue) conduction and through the air. (That’s probably why your recorded voice sounds so different from what you’re used to hearing when you talk.) Stick your fingers in your ears and speak out loud, and you’ll hear just the bone-conducted portion.

Bone conduction headphones take advantage of this phenomenon. Like all headphones, they have tiny little speakers. But instead of pointing those little speakers into our ear canals to vibrate the air and then our eardrums, the headphones are designed to press their little speakers against a bone—usually the cheekbone right in front of the ear. Technically, they are also conducting the sound through soft tissues like skin, muscle, and fat, but the bones do a really good job of transmitting sound and are what the technology is named after.

Yes, they work through actual bone conduction, but not only bone conduction. Some of the sound gets transmitted through the air as well. People don't always believe this. I've seen Reddit threads where people were arguing over whether bone conduction is bullshit, so here are two experiments you can do with bone conduction headphones to understand both parts of what’s going on.

First, wear them normally. The little speakers will be on the bony spot right in front of your ear. Turn on some music. Now pull the speakers gently away from your head, so they’re no longer making contact. Yes, you will still hear the music, but it will be tinny and quiet compared to when you were wearing them normally. This shows that bone conduction really is delivering a lot of the sound that you're hearing.

Now, wear them normally again, but plug your ears with your fingers (or, if you like, a handy pair of earplugs). The sound will be different—a bit deeper is how I would describe it. It almost seems like it gets louder. The headphones definitely don’t need air-based access to your eardrums to get sound through to you. This shows that with only bone conduction, you get most but not all of the sound from the headphones.

Some headphones use a hybrid approach on purpose. The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 headphones have an extra set of speakers for air-based transmission in addition to the speakers intended for bone conduction. This tends to give a better balance of frequencies, and thus better sound quality than headphones that use only bone conduction.

Bone conduction is neither better nor worse for your ears than traditional headphones, because ultimately the same thing happens in each: Your cochlea (which is the part of your ear that’s damaged in the most common types of hearing loss) receives the vibrations either way. Too-loud bone conduction headphones are bad for you, just like too-loud regular headphones.

There is one way that bone conduction headphones can be better for your ears, as I noted above: If you’re in a noisy environment, you can wear earplugs to protect your ears from the loud sounds around you, and you can wear bone-conduction headphones to deliver a bit of music to fill the silence.

I started wearing the earplugs-and-headphones combo this summer when I was doing a lot of outdoor workouts near a loud air conditioner (I also realized that the sound of dropping the bar was actually pretty darn loud as well, dropping the bar being a routine part of Olympic weightlifting). So I got some Loop earplugs, and found that not only could I still hear my music through my Aftershokz Aeropex Mini (an older version of what is now the Shokz OpenRun Mini), I was able to turn the volume to a near-minimum and still hear it just fine. Overall, my ears are getting a lot less noise exposure, so that’s a win-win.

There aren’t any health or safety downsides (as we discussed above), but you aren’t going to get pristine sound quality through bone conduction headphones. Some are better than others, and you should always check out reviews and try headphones in person if you want to make a buying decision based on sound quality. But in general, the upside of bone-conduction headphones is also their downside: Since Shokz and the like don’t block out ambient sounds, the sound that reaches your ear is a mix of the music you’re playing on purpose and the noises of the world around you.

When I wear bone conduction headphones with earplugs, I don’t get great sound quality either. Just like your voice sounds different with your ears plugged, the sound mix of bone conduction plus earplugs is not quite the same as what you’d hear through a good pair of quality headphones.

Personally, I find these minor downsides are balanced by the advantages that bone conduction headphones provide. I don’t need to hear my podcasts in crystal-clear audio while I’m running; I just want to be able to tell what the hosts are saying while also listening for approaching cars. When I do want to listen to music in high fidelity, I do that at home, with a nice pair of noise-canceling headphones.

title: GOP women sound alarm as Lindsay Clancy backlash revives calls to repeal 19th Amendment: ‘Definitely a threat’
description: Republican women warn that online calls to repeal the 19th Amendment after the Lindsay Clancy trial could alienate female voters from the GOP.
fullText:
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Calls to repeal women's rights to vote are emerging from the online firestorm over the Lindsay Clancy trial, prompting Republican women to warn that the intraparty rhetoric could hurt the GOP.

"I think there's definitely a threat in the Republican Party right now," political and legal strategist Mehek Cooke told Fox News Digital.

The online calls to repeal the 19th Amendment come after Clancy's high-profile murder trial ended in a mistrial, with 11 of the 12 jurors favoring a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity. Clancy admitted to killing her three children, but her defense argued she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Lindsay Clancy Mistrial Declared After Jury Deadlocks In Killings Of Her Three Children

"Convict Clancy. Also Repeal the 19th Amendment!" one user posted on X.

"The female jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial are speaking out about their deliberations and disagreements with the sole male holdout. The more they speak the better they make the case for repealing the 19th Amendment," another user posted.

Cooke warned that calls to strip women of the right to vote, largely coming from accounts identifying as conservative, risk alienating female voters from the Republican Party.

"When you have these fringe activists online talking about repealing the 19th Amendment or alienating women, it really doesn't help," Cooke said.

The calls followed after the case made waves on social media, particularly after hundreds of mostly female Clancy supporters gathered outside a Massachusetts courthouse during the murder trial. The demonstrators rallying behind Clancy argued the case is an example of the lack of understanding of postpartum depression.

Rogan Shreds Supporters Of Lindsay Clancy, Says They Wouldn't Rally If A Father Were On Trial For Same Crime

But the demonstrations quickly turned into ammunition for online critics who argued that the support for Clancy is an indication that women should be stripped of their right to vote.

"This Lindsay Clancy trial has shown us How spiteful women can be, the fact that women are willing to even defend a child killer just because they want to be ok with the "sisterhood" should alarm you," another user wrote on X.

"They will gaslight you, they will use sign language against you and even try to call you all sort of names. But guess what, they are still wrong and they know it. Repeal the 19th."

Cooke pushed back on the idea that the calls to repeal the 19th Amendment reflect the reality of the mainstream Republican Party.

"Social media isn't real life," Cooke said. "I think a lot of people out there put these arbitrary crazy ideas, but it doesn't really reflect what normal people think and what mainstream thinks.

Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial Becomes Social Media Obsession As Tiktokers, Sleuths Debate Controversial Case

"I think you're getting these calls because of where our culture is today. You looked at the Lindsay Clancy trial and all the women out there in pink that were continuing to support a woman who murdered three children. You're constantly seeing this cultural push in terms of where women stand today in politics."

Tiffany Losee, director of fundraising for The Conservative Caucus, told Fox News Digital that Democrats are to blame for pushing out this agenda and associating it with the broader Republican Party.

"You have to understand this is all a game to the Democrat Party," Losee said. "They're going to push out anything that looks fringe on the right."

Losee also claimed that Democrats are using this rhetoric on the right to distract voters from the rise of socialism that has emerged within the Democratic Party, claiming if voters understood the ideals of the party, they would "run faster than imaginable to get away from such government control."

How The 'Long March' Through The Institutions Led To Socialist Takeover Of Dem Party: 'Need To Wake Up'

"They're gonna push out crazy Lindsay Clancy ideas or 'look over here at something shiny, or communism is cool, socialism is cool, everything's free,'" Losee said. "But then they will not take that extra step to educate the voter on what exactly they are pushing."

Cooke and Losee spoke to Fox News Digital on the issue as Republicans gathered in Dallas for the party's first-ever midterm convention, where the GOP gathered to rally its base to vote as Republicans work to stay in control of Congress as November's midterm elections approach.

"I think the left has constantly alienated women," Cooke said. "It's our responsibility to pull them in and show them common sense."

Original article

title: Iran denounces Austria for blocking its nuclear chief from a meeting in Vienna
description: Iran on Monday condemned the exclusion of the head of its Atomic Energy Organization from the annual gathering of the United Nations nuclear agency in Vienna saying that it constitutes “a serious brea...
fullText:
VIENNA (AP) — Iran on Monday condemned the exclusion of the head of its Atomic Energy Organization from the annual gathering of the United Nations nuclear agency in Vienna saying that it constitutes "a serious breach" of Tehran's rights as a member nation.

"By obstructing our full and effective participation, the denial of access contravenes both the letter and the spirit of the legal framework" governing attendance at meetings of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran's ambassador to the agency, Reza Najafi, told delegates at its general conference.

Najafi criticized Austria, the host country of the IAEA and other U.N. organizations, saying that Vienna's decision not to grant a visa to Mohammad Eslami "violates the host country's obligation."

The Russian ambassador to the U.N. in Vienna, Mikhail Ulyanov, echoed Iran's remarks, saying that Austria had "grossly violated" its obligations as host nation of the IAEA.

Western nations had "unleashed a genuine campaign of visa-related abuses so as to settle scores with countries they deem to be undesirable," he said.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei on Monday likewise condemned Austria's refusal to issue a visa to Eslami.

Baghaei said Tehran protested the decision and summoned the Austrian chargé d'affaires, saying Austria was obligated as the host country to issue the visas.

Austria responded by saying a U.N. Security Council committee had rejected Austria's request to exempt Eslami from the travel ban.

"As a consequence, Austria was obliged to deny one member of the Iranian delegation the entry into its territory," said Christian Ebner, Austria's ambassador to the IAEA.

As the host of international organizations, Austria can request exemptions from travel bans to enable sanctioned officials to attend international conferences at the U.N. in Vienna.

The decision whether to grant the waiver rests with the U.N. Security Council's sanctions committee.

The committee is responsible for overseeing the punitive measures reimposed last year after France, Britain and Germany triggered the so-called snapback mechanism that automatically reinstated all United Nations sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program.

The reinstated sanctions include a travel ban, a conventional arms embargo, restrictions on ballistic missile development, asset freezes and a ban on producing nuclear-related technology.

Iran, Russia and China reject the legality of the sanctions reimposed under the snapback mechanism.

The U.S. ambassador to the U.N. in Vienna, Preston Wells Griffith, said Austria's exemption request was denied after Washington lodged an objection with the committee.

"While we are focused on a diplomatic solution to the challenges posed by Iran's nuclear program, we could not allow a U.N. designated official to travel … without any meaningful cooperation on nuclear safeguards," he said.

Since Israel and the U.S. struck Iran's nuclear sites during the 12-day war in June 2025, Iran hasn't given IAEA inspectors access to the affected sites — even though Tehran is legally obliged to cooperate with the watchdog under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.

The IAEA has also been unable to verify the status of a stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the June bombing. According to the IAEA, Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.

The U.N. atomic watchdog's board earlier this month adopted a resolution reporting Iran to the U.N. Security Council for the first time in 20 years because of its failure to cooperate citing in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.

Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons program until 2003. Iran says that it's not pursuing nuclear weapons, and that its program is entirely peaceful.

title: He had a gig mowing lawns at 11. By 25, he had turned it into a multimillion-dollar landscaping business.
description: Cody Kuebler began by cutting his neighbors' grass for about $25 a lawn. Now, at 25 years old, he oversees a $4.5 million landscaping business.
fullText:
He began by cutting neighbors' grass for about $25 a lawn.

A move at 14 meant rebuilding his customer base from scratch.

He now oversees millions of dollars' worth of equipment — and works six days a week.

Some kids mow lawns for pocket money and move on. Cody Kuebler kept at it, turning the childhood gig into a multimillion-dollar business.

Now 25, Kuebler said he spent his summers growing up cutting his neighbors' grass for around $25 a job, first with an aging push mower, and later with one his father gave him for his 11th birthday. The gift involved "a little bit of horse-trading," he said: He'd have to cut his dad's lawn.

Along the way, he hired friends so he could take on more customers and expand into snow removal during the winter months. Eventually, he earned enough to invest in riding lawn mowers with wagons attached.

"I got a little taste of earning money and being my own boss," Kuebler told Business Insider. "That kind of stuck in my head."

Business Insider's Young Geniuses series spotlights the next generation of founders, innovators, and thinkers trying to reshape industries and solve global challenges. See more stories from the series here, or reach out to editor Peter Gelling to share your story.

Getting to where he is today, though, took grit and determination. Kuebler's parents divorced when he was 10, and a few years later, he moved from his childhood home in a small Iowa town to Des Moines after his father got a new job there. That meant having to start his fledgling business all over again.

"It was frustrating because I had built a decent amount of customers that I lost over a decision I didn't make and couldn't change," Kuebler said.

He pressed ahead, though as high school graduation approached, Kuebler wasn't sure his business could lead to a career. Since he is a car enthusiast and had already earned enough credits to graduate, he said he spent part of his senior year studying diesel mechanics at a local community college. He dropped out during the first semester, concluding he'd spent enough time in the classroom.

Kuebler also considered working in sales. He got a job at a tire shop, but said his boss wasn't interested in pursuing ideas he had to grow the business. That experience clarified his own ambitions.

"I always knew I wanted to do 

So Kuebler quit the tire shop to focus on his lawn-mowing and snow-removal venture, starting by setting it up as a limited liability company, or LLC, called CLK Landscape Construction. It was March 2020, a time that turned out to be ideal, as the pandemic was getting underway. Over the next two years, sales ballooned nearly ninefold to around $730,000.

title: GAA remains committed to integration process - Burns
description: GAA President Jarlath Burns insists the process of integration between Gaelic games' three bodies is not over but the key is to ensure the outcome is "sustainable and robust".
fullText:
GAA President Jarlath Burns insists the process of integration between Gaelic games' three bodies is not over but the key is to ensure the outcome is "sustainable and robust".

Last week, former Irish president Dr Mary McAleese stepped down from the role as chairperson of the steering group to oversee the planned merger of the Gaelic Athletic Association, Camogie Association and Ladies Gaelic Football Association [LGFA] with the 2027 deadline for completion set to be missed.

Dr McAleese said she was "dubious" whether there was real desire from the GAA to make it happen but the current GAA president - speaking at the Hurling Development Committee's starter pack launch for 2026 in Belcoo - denies the issue is dead in the water.

"There was an idea going around last week that integration had stopped - it hasn't," Burns told BBC Sport NI's Mark Sidebottom.

"Integration is happening every day. We see examples here where boys and girls are playing hurling and camogie together. That's going on in every club every day and every decision we make at the moment, we're making it from an integrated perspective.

"The three organisations are still very committed to integration, but we want to achieve an integration that is sustainable and robust, and something we can be very proud of."

Last week, GAA director general Tom Ryan said the initial timescale had proven to be "a little bit too ambitious" and Burns says the missed deadline is "disappointing", it "doesn't end the process".

"We will get back up and running and we have already been in talks with Camogie [Association] and LGFA last week," he confirmed.

"We will continue to do so until we get the integration where every boy and every girl has the equality of opportunity and can enjoy Gaelic games in the future."

title: Mahmoud Khalil lawsuit says Columbia failed to protect pro-Palestinian activists
description: Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil sued Columbia University on Monday, alleging it failed to address harassment against him and other members of a pro-Palestinian campus group and retaliated against ...
fullText:
Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil sued Columbia University on Monday, alleging it failed to address harassment against him and other members of a pro-Palestinian campus group and retaliated against them when they reported it.

The university's "deliberate indifference" led to the doxing of multiple group members and Khalil's detention by immigration agents, according to the civil rights lawsuit filed in federal court in New York City.

At a news conference announcing the lawsuit, Khalil accused the university of "discrimination aimed at intimidating Palestinian students."

"We are suing because no student, regardless of their background, should go through the hell that Columbia put us through over all these years," he said.

The university declined to comment on the lawsuit, but said in an email that "creating a campus environment where every member of our community feels welcome, supported, and safe is fundamental to who we are as a University."

"Columbia is committed to protecting our community from discrimination and harassment, and responding promptly and appropriately when concerns arise," it said.

Khalil also sued Columbia last year to block the release of student records to a congressional committee.

A former graduate student at Columbia University, Khalil gained prominence as a spokesperson for student activists protesting Israel's actions in Gaza.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested him at his apartment on campus in March 2025, and he quickly became the face of the Trump administration's crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrators.

Khalil spent 104 days in a Louisiana immigration jail, missing the birth of his first child, before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered his release. His deportation case remains active.

Khalil's latest lawsuit says Columbia "refused to correct disinformation" while he was detained, "allowing a false narrative about his conduct and role to persist and further enabling peer-on-peer harassment of other Palestinian students and students with perceived shared Arab and/or Muslim ancestry."

Instead of investigating reports of harassment, the university retaliated by characterizing events by a pro-Palestinian campus group as security risks and revising disciplinary policy to target criticism of the Israeli government, according to the lawsuit.

At the news conference Monday, Khalil also accused the university of surveilling pro-Palestinian students and hiring private investigators to monitor him.

The lawsuit accuses Columbia of civil rights violations, requests a court order restoring Khalil's access to the campus and ending the Palestinian group's suspension, and seeks damages "to be determined at trial."

It also names the pro-Palestinian group and its president, Mohammad Zubairi, as plaintiffs.

title: Inside House Republicans' plan to end run Dem opposition and pass Trump-backed voter ID
description: Congressional Republicans plan to bypass the Senate filibuster and pass the SAVE America Act's voter ID and proof of citizenship rules via reconciliation.
fullText:
Congressional Republicans have a plan to pass key portions of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act before the end of this year.

The election integrity bill backed by President Donald Trump and fiercely opposed by Democrats has stalled in Congress, where Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been reluctant to call it up for a vote, given that it's all but assured to fail.

At least several Democrats would be needed to reach the Senate's 60-vote threshold to break a filibuster. But left-wing lawmakers in the House and Senate have panned the legislation as an attempt to sow doubt in U.S. elections at best and voter suppression at worst.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is now pushing Republicans to pass the bill's main mandates via the budget reconciliation process, which allows the party in power to pass sweeping fiscal policy without input from the minority due to its sidelining of the Senate filibuster. Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., chairman of the Committee on House Administration, is tasked with overseeing how that part of the bill gets done.

Trump Questions Thune's Leadership As Save America Act Stalls

"I'd rather pass the SAVE America Act. But recognizing that the Senate might not be able to get that done with the 60-vote threshold, let's leverage the parliamentary procedure, bring that threshold down to 50, and get some really commonsense reforms done," Steil told Fox News Digital in an interview. "I've been having great conversations with my colleagues in the administration as well as the Senate."

Senate Faces 'Come-to-jesus' Moment On Trump's Election Priority Under Gop's New Plan

Steil told Fox News Digital that he hoped Congress could pass a reconciliation bill with SAVE America before the November midterm elections, but conceded "the clock is ticking down pretty quickly."

The budget reconciliation process is a lengthy one, with Republicans having taken roughly half a year to use it to pass Trump's signature One Big, Beautiful Bill Act last year. Both the House and Senate must pass budget "frameworks," with instructions for relevant committees to enact policies that either spend or cut funding to a specified amount.

Those committees pass their portions, then send them back to the House and Senate budget committees to tie them together into one massive bill. Identical bills must pass the House and Senate before getting to Trump's desk.

Steil's panel, which has jurisdiction over federal election law, is aiming to include two portions of the original SAVE America Act: a proof of citizenship mandate for the voter registration process, and a nationwide photo ID rule to cast a ballot.

Read The Documents: White House Releases Election Integrity Files After Trump Speech

"The House can go as fast as the Senate. And so the frustration that I and others have is the Senate's not moving as fast as we would like on this. I actually think there's 50 votes in the Senate for some of these really commonsense provisions," Steil said. "I'd like to be sooner rather than later, but I don't control them."

Where the process gets even trickier is when the Senate parliamentarian, who is appointed by Senate leadership to help interpret the chamber's rules, goes through the reconciliation bill draft and weeds out what does not adhere to the process rules. That means anything that does not impact the federal government's budget, tax policy, or the national debt is generally removed.

Top Trump Official Makes New Save Act Case To Republicans Behind Closed Doors

Steil said portions of the SAVE America Act could arguably get through that filtration process by affecting funds going to states via the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), a 2002-era election reform law.

"We could free up those funds or enhance those funds for states to do those post-election audits, which is a really important part of election integrity. You can do the same in regards to photo ID," he said, adding that making Real ID the standard could also effectively impact the citizenship mandate. "Effectively, when an individual gets REAL ID, they're proving their citizenship."

Trump Intervenes As House Gop Revolt Puts Save America Act At Center Of Spending Showdown

And the Trump administration is behind the push. Earlier this year, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought told Republicans at a lawmaker-only meeting that the White House backed using the reconciliation process for SAVE America and argued it was the best way forward to pass the GOP's election reforms, multiple people in the room told Fox News Digital.

"The White House is engaged. We've had good conversations," Steil told Fox News Digital.

The House passed its version of the reconciliation bill earlier this summer, a $95 billion budget aimed at replenishing the U.S. military and enhancing election security.

But in the Senate, Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled his committee's framework just before the chamber left for the August recess. It's not clear when it will advance through his panel or get a vote.

Gop Civil War Erupts Over Trump's Latest Agenda Push As Key Republicans Threaten To Sink Megabill

Their legislation calls for up to $150 billion in spending — a significant difference.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., acknowledged that gap in an interview with Fox News Digital last month.

"I mean, the idea was, in keeping it skinny, is to move it quickly. And so the more you add to it, the more complex it gets, the 

Steil said he was optimistic that an agreement could be reached.

"I think, broadly, we're aligned. I think obviously the total numbers are different," he said. "I think everyone recognizes the importance of making sure that our men and women in uniform have the resources needed to not only defend themselves but to defend our country... And also that we have the resources needed to make sure that we're protecting our election."

title: Pollock still 'open to new opportunities' as Northampton talks go on
description: Henry Pollock continues to play hardball in his negotiations over a Northampton Saints contract extension, insisting he is still open to offers from elsewhere.
fullText:
Henry Pollock continues to play hardball in his negotiations over a Northampton Saints contract extension, insisting he is still open to offers from elsewhere, including overseas, and that he remains determined to be "quite selfish" over his future.

The 21-year-old England back row's current deal, thought to be worth about £150,000 a year, expires at the end of the forthcoming campaign.

Pollock added Eddie Hearn to his advisory team earlier this year and the boxing impresario upped the ante by claiming his new client was "a seven-figure player", whose current pay shocked him.

"Northampton's been so great to me, I've been here my whole career and they've made me who I am. For me to stay here would be so special," said Pollock.

"Obviously, I know it's not as easy as that and I know there's lots of moving parts that come into play. I'm very open to new opportunities and I'm very open to exploring that.

"I'm so young so I think it's only right that I assess those options and find the best decision for myself."

He added: "Your career is so short that you look back on yourself and you almost regret not exploring new avenues, exploring different things.

"I think for me, you almost have to be quite selfish in that aspect, think what's right for you. If that is staying here, then that's great, I'll be here for however long. If it's not, then I'll be open to new opportunities."

Salary cap rules, which prevent players moving between Prem clubs from being designated as 'marquee' players whose pay is exempt from a £6.4m squad limit, make a big-money move to one of Saints' domestic rivals difficult.

A move to a club in France or Japan would potentially be lucrative to Pollock, and a deal which began at the start of the 2027-28 season would not rule him out of contention for England's Rugby World Cup squad next autumn.

However, he would become ineligible for England once he begins playing overseas and would lose the central contract, worth about £150,000 a year, that currently tops up his club wages.

His off-pitch earnings - he has personal endorsement deals with various clothing brands - might also suffer away from the exposure of the Test arena and domestic rugby.

"I definitely want to go and live in different countries, explore new sports, explore new avenues," said Pollock.

"Again, that's all down to the management team. I'm just speaking to them loads and assessing my options and seeing what's right for myself."

Northampton, who have reportedly made an offer that would raise Pollock's pay to £400,000 a year,, external remain confident they will secure an extension.

Saints allowed club captain George Furbank to leave for Harlequins in the summer, conscious that a raft of young stars in their title-winning team were due a pay rise.

Fly-half Fin Smith agreed a new deal in October, while wing Tommy Freeman is in line for his own new deal this season. Scrum-half Archie McParland and prop Emmanuel Iyogun are also priorities to tie down to new contracts.

"We're getting closer," said director of rugby Phil Dowson on a deal with Pollock.

"As you can imagine, it's complex. There's a few moving parts that we need to put together, but I'm hopeful. As I said before, he wants to stay and we want to keep him.

"Obviously there's some negotiations going between that but those two things are very positive."

title: Joe Manchin says he supports Republican candidates in battleground Senate races in Maine and Michigan
description: Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin, a Democrat-turned-independent, said Monday he supports two Republican Senate candidates running in battleground races in November.
fullText:
Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin, a Democrat-turned-independent, said Monday he supports two Republican Senate candidates running in battleground races in November.

During an appearance on CNBC, Manchin expressed support for former Rep. Mike Rogers, who is running for an open seat in Michigan, and Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who is seeking reelection. Both races are crucial to whether the GOP will retain control of the Senate.

"You lose the Susan Collinses of the Senate, you're losing the soul of the Senate — basically, a person you can talk to, who wants to do the right thing all of the time," Manchin said, adding that he would campaign with the senator.

Manchin, a longtime critic of extremes in both parties, served in the Senate from 2010-2025 and left the Democratic Party during his final months in office, arguing that the party's brand had become "toxic." He has remained involved in politics and launched a national effort in July to help elect more independents.

In the CNBC interview, Manchin praised Collins, Rogers and Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who is not up for reelection until 2028, as "independent, free-thinking Republicans, not completely crazy right or completely crazy left."

Manchin previously crossed party lines as a Democrat in the Senate to support Collins in her last reelection campaign.

As for Michigan, Manchin said he hasn't made any endorsements but called Rogers a "personal friend" and expressed a preference for him as the show's host asked about Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken progressive.

"I do support Mike Rogers," Manchin said. "I think Mike Rogers is a good person. I think he'll do a great job."

At the same time, Manchin said Rogers "has to" denounce President Donald Trump's trade policies to win his race, something the candidate has not done. "We'll have to see," Manchin said.

In Maine, Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, the former state Senate president who replaced embattled nominee Graham Platner on the ballot, as she fights for a sixth term in a state that Trump has lost three times. She highlighted Manchin's remarks on social media and in a news release and said she was "honored" to have his support.

"Joe is a dear friend and trusted colleague with whom I have always worked closely to solve problems and deliver results for the people of Maine and America," Collins said.

In CNN polling released Wednesday, both the Maine and Michigan races were close, with no clear leader among likely voters.

title: Police officer who put suspect in headlock and punched him 9 times faces misconduct hearing
description: PC Richard Williams faces eight allegations relating to an arrest in a police misconduct hearing.
fullText:
PC Richard Williams was filmed punching a suspect with one hand as he gripped the man's neck with his other arm

A police officer who punched a suspect nine times in the head used unreasonable force on multiple occasions, a police misconduct hearing has been told.

PC Richard Williams faces eight allegations relating to the arrest of Steven Clark, including using a headlock or "choker", unreasonable use of incapacitant spray, and throwing or dropping Clark into the back of a police van.

A misconduct hearing at North Wales Police headquarters in Colwyn Bay heard Williams denies wrongdoing.

He was cleared of assault and intentional strangulation following a seven-day trial in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, in 2025.

In May 2023, police were called to Porthmadog in Gwynedd, following a report of a domestic argument.

A woman told officers, Clark, then 34, was "off his head on wacky backy" and possibly other drugs.

The misconduct hearing was played several clips of police body-worn camera footage, as well as mobile phone video recorded by onlookers.

When police tried to arrest Clark, the misconduct hearing was told things "take a turn", and the suspect ended up on the ground.

It is alleged Williams used handcuffs to "cause pain to Clark's wrist", who "winced and reacted".

It is also alleged he put Clark in a headlock, which it is claimed was "unreasonable".

Clark claimed he "could not breathe", and later suggested during police interview he was losing consciousness.

It is also claimed Clark "is punched by Williams nine times in the face or head", and that "punching Clark nine times in the face was not a reasonable use of force".

The hearing was told "it is nine pretty quick punches" with no pause for reflection.

Four allegations relate to the use, or apparent use, of incapacitant spray.

Another is that Clark was "thrown or dropped into the van" while trying to resist.

It is claimed the eight allegations "amount to an unreasonable use of force".

The hearing was adjourned until Tuesday.

title: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr accuses James Talarico of running a 'hoax' over equal time statute
description: Brendan Carr accuses James Talarico of running a "hoax" by banking on public confusion over the equal time statute to drive clicks and donations.
fullText:
Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr accused Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico of banking on public confusion over the equal time statute to drive clicks and donations.

Last week, Talarico appeared on ABC's "Jimmy Kimmel Live!," but the liberal late-night host insisted the interview had to air on YouTube, instead of broadcast television, because the FCC has "threatened" the network.

The White House previously said Kimmel was "play-acting," because the FCC did not threaten him regarding interviewing Talarico, or any other candidate.

Carr responded on Saturday to an account on X that complained Talarico was relegated to YouTube, but Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, was allowed to appear on ESPN's "College Gameday." The chairman blasted Talarico, noting that the equal time statute doesn't apply to ESPN and does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast TV.

Kimmel Reveals He's Interviewing James Talarico Under 'Unusual Circumstances,' Citing Fcc Threats

"It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others. Indeed, when the statute applies, it simply requires broadcast stations to offer comparable time and placement. And comparable does not necessarily mean an interview by the same person on the same program either," Carr wrote.

"This ties back to Talarico," Carr continued. "He's just running the same hoax he did a few months ago on Colbert for the purpose of getting clicks and donations — he's banking on people not understanding the statute or operating as partisan lemmings."

Democratic Rep Tells Abc, Cbs To 'Grow A Spine' After Kimmel Announces Alternative Talarico Interview

Former late-night host Stephen Colbert interviewed Talarico in February, ahead of the Texas Senate primary, in which he was competing against Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett.

Colbert's show, which has since been canceled, did not air the interview with Talarico and only posted it to the show's YouTube channel in February. Colbert announced at the time that CBS had stopped them from airing the interview.

Jimmy Kimmel Reveals He Asked Major Trump Critic To Guest Host While He's On Vacation As A 'Special Treat'

Crockett, who ultimately lost the Senate primary to Talarico, blamed CBS and Colbert's show. Critics on social media noted that Talarico's sit-down with Kimmel was similar to the Colbert edition, with both hosts setting the Senate candidate up to declare that the Trump administration must be scared of him if they're taking equal time so seriously.

The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

In Saturday's post, Carr also explained that "cable shows are different than broadcast programs."

"Broadcasters are unique. The FCC gave them free licenses worth many billions of dollars to use a public resource (spectrum). They are given a government-sanctioned monopoly on their broadcast frequencies, too. If anyone else wants to use that same public resource (spectrum) for the purpose of expressing their own views, the government will not let them — it will eject anyone else that tries to use a broadcaster's licensed spectrum," he wrote.

"This means that Americans are subsidizing the distribution of broadcast programs over a public resource to the tune of many billions of dollars. We don't do that with cable or anything else. In exchange for that free and exclusive right to use spectrum, broadcasters made a deal with the American people," Carr continued. "They agreed to operate, not in their own narrow interests, but in the public interest. There are various rules and policies that they must follow. This sets them apart from newspapers and cable shows and podcasts."

Kimmel's interview with Talarico has piled up over 9 million views on YouTube.

title: What Carlos Alcaraz has done since losing in the US Open quarterfinals to Ben Shelton
description: Though he did not manage to defend his title, it’s fair to say it was a successful US Open for Carlos Alcaraz. After being sidelined...
fullText:
Though he did not manage to defend his title, it's fair to say it was a successful US Open for Carlos Alcaraz.

After being sidelined with a wrist injury for four months, Alcaraz made his eagerly anticipated return to professional tennis at Flushing Meadows, much to the delight of every fan.

The Spaniard kicked off his US Open by competing in the mixed doubles event alongside Serena Williams and picked up a victory with the legendary 23-time major winner.

Following the highs of witnessing his comeback with Williams, many felt an announcement of Alcaraz's withdrawal from US Open singles was inevitable.

But the world number three went through with his plans to defend his title, and he did not disappoint.

Alcaraz dropped just one set en route to the quarterfinals of the US Open, which he conceded in the second round to Jaime Faria.

He beat 20th seed Tommy Paul to book his place in the last eight, where he was ultimately knocked out by Ben Shelton in a thrilling five-setter.

After losing to the American, it was revealed by Spanish outlet Marca that Alcaraz returned to training on Sunday.

The 23-year-old, back on the practice courts this week, was focusing on physical conditioning ahead of the Laver Cup in London, his next event.

The Laver Cup gets underway on the 25th of September, with Alcaraz headlining the star-studded lineup.

Alcaraz will play for Team Europe alongside Alexander Zverev, Rafael Jodar, Flavio Cobolli, Jakub Mensik and Casper Ruud.

Team World will be represented by Shelton, Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur, Alexander Bublik, Learner Tien and Francisco Cerundolo.

Alcaraz made his Laver Cup debut at the 2024 edition of the annual team event and lost his first match there in doubles with Zverev as his partner against the duo of Shelton and Fritz.

He then got two points on the board in his singles match on day two that year by beating Shelton before helping Team Europe clinch the victory on day three by defeating Fritz in singles and winning his doubles match with Ruud against Shelton and Frances Tiafoe.

Team Europe denied Team World a three-peat in 2024, but the latter recaptured the cup in 2025.

Alcaraz won his opening doubles match in 2025 but suffered a shocking defeat to Fritz on day two in singles.

On day three, he emerged victorious in another doubles match and beat Cerundolo in singles, but it was not enough for Team Europe.

In total, Team Europe have won the Laver Cup five times since its inaugural edition in 2017, with Team World having hoisted the trophy three times.

title: Bremer spoke with Juventus stars to convince them to stay this season
description: Gleison Bremer is one of the best players at Juventus, and he is also one of the leaders in the Bianconeri dressing room. As a result, he is highly respected by his teammates and is using that influen...
fullText:
Gleison Bremer is one of the best players at Juventus, and he is also one of the leaders in the Bianconeri dressing room. As a result, he is highly respected by his teammates and is using that influence to good effect.

The defender has now revealed that he spoke to Douglas Luiz and Nicolas Gonzalez about staying at the club during the summer, when both players were expected to leave.

Juventus had been open to both players leaving for the right price, after they spent last season on loan at different clubs. The Bianconeri were prepared for the possibility of losing them and believed they could still perform well if the departures happened.

Gonzalez did not want to play for Juventus again, while Luiz was open to leaving if an offer arrived. However, the Brazilian became more open to remaining after none of his loan clubs completed a permanent deal for him.

Luiz now wants stability and an opportunity to prove that he can perform well in Turin. Meanwhile, Gonzalez was forced to remain at Juventus because there was no serious offer for his signature during the last transfer window.

Bremer spoke to both players in an effort to convince them to stay, highlighting the importance of their presence to the team. The defender believes they can make a significant contribution during the campaign.

(Photo by Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images)

Bremer revealed through Calciomercato:

"I spoke to them, especially with Nico and also with Douglas; they are important players who have character, they have strength, and they will help us do what we have to do this year."

The comments show the role Bremer has taken within the Juventus dressing room, particularly when it comes to encouraging his teammates to remain committed to the club.

Both Luiz and Gonzalez will now have the opportunity to contribute to Juventus after remaining at the club. Bremer clearly believes their character and strength can help the Bianconeri achieve what they need to accomplish this year.

title: MLB Mid-September Check-in: AL West
description: Wake me up when September ends.
fullText:
Every day, Pinstripe Alley offers updates on what the Yankees' top American League opponents are up to through the Rivalry Roundup. The AL East is well-trodden ground there, but with the final month of the season just ahead, we're going to take a peek around MLB as a whole and check in with each of the other five divisions. Who's surprising? Who's underwhelming? Who's simply mediocre at the moment? Read on and find out.

Top Position Player: Yordan Alvarez (5.8 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Peter Lambert (2.4 fWAR)

Much like a panicked squashed cockroach in a muggy South Texas roadside motel, the Astros currently find themselves right at .500 but somehow leading the division. What I mean is they're barely alive, but still living their dream in a division that is a trashcan.

The rest of the way the Astros start with four games at home versus lowly Kansas City and then welcome the NL East leading Braves to Space City for a three game set. Houston then finishes the year with two games in Seattle before finishing the season with a four-game set with the Athletics.

Houston might very well walk away from what should be a disappointing season in terms of record with a division crown, triple-crown winner, and possible MVP. Why the baseball Gods feel inclined to continue to bless this abomination of a ball club is beyond me.

Top Position Player: Ezequiel Durán (4.7 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Jacob deGrom (4.1 fWAR)

The other Texas team came into the month with a chance to run down their instate foes but have not done anything to make it easier on themselves after starting September 5-6. The odds makers currently have the Rangers' playoffs chances around 30 percent. And it might just be recency bias, but the Rangers seem like the hottest team out west with their current two-game win streak.

The Rangers' next game kicks off a nine game homestand. The Red Sox are the first team to come to town, followed by the Blue Jays, and then the Mets crash the party. All three series are three games apiece. The Rangers then close the season in Minnesota with another three game set against the Twins.

Not having a single game left against the AL West hurts the Rangers chances to run down the Astros. Another Texas-sized problem for the Rangers is the fact their lone star neighbors hold the tiebreaker so they are really an additional game back in the standings. With 12 games left to go will the Rangers be able to free the world from having to watch the Astros in the playoffs?

Top Position Player: Randy Arozarena (4.3 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Bryan Woo (3.7 fWAR)

While I would say the Tigers have to hold the torch for the most disappointing team in 2026, the Mariners might be the challenger for that top spot. Seattle's sky high expectations are all but sleepless at this point, unless they find some magic and get some help.

In order to reach the .500 mark, that might be all that is needed to win the west, the Mariners would need to be near perfect. They honestly have the schedule to pull it off, but it is hard to sweep teams. Starting today the Mariners are in LA for three games against the Angels, then shoot over to Denver to face the punching bag of a club in the Rockies for three games. Seattle returns home for the final six, with two against the Astros, before getting the Angels for the last four games of the season.

The Mariners have already clinched the tiebreaker versus the Astros on the season. It is very unlikely, but having the tiebreaker is huge and if the Astros slip the Mariners very well could be the team that squeaks their way into the division crown.

Top Position Player: Nick Kurtz (2.6 fWAR)
Top Pitchers: J.T. Ginn (1.7 fWAR)

The team formerly from Oakland always comes into the season looking at true two outcomes. They either surprise and find themselves at the top of the division with players to be traded later, or they bottom out like they did this season. The Athletics have one more year before relocating to Vegas.

On a Yankees note, the Athletics are our second favorite team this week as they face the Rays starting on Tuesday for a three game set in the Trop. It might be a bad bet, but maybe the Athletics will be able to channel ghosts of decades past and take one or two games before leaving Florida.

Top Position Players: Mike Trout and Zach Neto (3.3 fWAR)
Top Pitcher: Reid Detmers (4.4 fWAR)

The Angels might finally, ironically, have a light at the end of the tunnel as they will be under new ownership after the 2026 season. Change cannot come fast enough for the team battling the Rockies for the league's worst record.

title: Emma Raducanu’s former coach issues defence of Alexander Zverev and insists he plays within the rules
description: Alexander Zverev may have just won the US Open title, but the reaction has been far from overwhelmingly positive. After all, one negative narrative that...
fullText:
Alexander Zverev may have just won the US Open title, but the reaction has been far from overwhelmingly positive.

After all, one negative narrative that really picked up as he went through the competition surrounded his serve, and particularly how long it took him to toss the ball.

It was stated that he had bounced the ball roughly 12,000 times before the semi-final, and during the final, the umpire had to warn him for taking too long between serves.

Ben Shelton has discussed this controversy surrounding Zverev already following his loss, whilst others have called for a rule change because of it.

However, Mark Petchey has now leapt to his defence.

Taking to X, he began with a rather controversial, contrary stance to which most have been taking.

The former coach of Emma Raducanu simply wrote: "I love the fact that @AlexZverev plays within the rules."

Petchey then explained why: "One of the very few players who walks around the net after the first game and at the changeovers in tiebreaks.

"Serves within 25 seconds. The ball bouncing isn't the issue. It's the 70% plus 1st serves in that's the problem for everyone.

"Overcome some absolutely brutal heartbreaking losses. Granite mentality and work ethic. Double Major winner in a season Hall of Fame career incoming.

Interestingly, Juan Martin del Potro briefly gave his opinion on this during the US Open final.

Speaking live on ESPN, just after Alexander Zverev had complained about being given a warning, the Argentinian took an interesting standpoint.

He argued: "The only reason she said that is that Zverev is playing Shelton. He's played six matches, nobody has said anything… until now."

That being said, Zverev was also warned during his match against Karen Khachanov, with the Russian also expressing his annoyance afterwards.

title: Alexander Zverev Pokes Fun at Trinity Rodman After Defeating Her Boyfriend Ben Shelton in US Open Final
description: The German tennis star won his second Grand Slam title after besting Shelton at Arthur Ashe Stadium
fullText:
Alexander Zverev had jokes after winning the US Open

The German tennis star engaged in a back-and-forth with Trinity Rodman, who is his opponent Ben Shelton's girlfriend

"Trinity, I thought you have a game today," he said to the Washington Spirit forward, who was seated in Shelton's players box

Moments after winning his first Grand Slam title, Alexander Zverev took time to acknowledge an unlikely fan in the crowd.

"Trinity, I thought you have a game today," Zverev, 29, joked to his opponent Ben Shelton's girlfriend. "Well done to you as well. You're the lucky charm ... not today, but usually."

Rodman, 24, joined in on laughing with the crowd good-naturedly, as she wiped away tears after her boyfriend's loss to the German, 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Shelton's appearance marked the first time that a Black American man competed in the US Open final since the stadium's namesake, Arthur Ashe, did so in 1972.

Zverev dominated much of the match, allowing Shelton, 23, only one set.

The 2026 French Open winner — known for his trademark serve which comes after he bounces the ball upwards of 20 times on the court — also took time to acknowledge Shelton's father and coach, Bryan Shelton.

Zverev was seen hugging the former ATP tour player, as well as Shelton's other coaches, after clinching his second Grand slam win.

For Rodman, the emotional day started in the nation's capital, where her Washington Spirit took on the Boston Legacy, losing 0-3.

Despite the 1 p.m. ET start, the soccer star was able to travel to New York City after the game, where she caught the end of Shelton's match.

"It means everything," Shelton, 23, said. "I knew she was coming — I knew it was going to be pretty close to impossible to get here. Even making the effort and trying is insane."

title: What Cam Heyward told refs after controversial Steelers penalty
description: Pittsburgh Steelers captain Cam Heyward shares his on-field exchange with game officials following a questionable defensive holding call.
fullText:
While the Pittsburgh Steelers secured a 20–13 victory over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 1, longtime defensive leader Cameron Heyward was far from satisfied with everything that transpired on the field.

Speaking on his podcast, "Not Just Football with Cam Heyward," the veteran defensive lineman voiced extreme frustration over a defensive holding call whistled against Pittsburgh during a direct, downhill run play. Both Yahya Black and Derrick Harmon were flagged by officials for defensive holding on consecutive defensive drives within a span of just a few plays.

Unwilling to let the officiating crew off the hook, Heyward detailed how he directly confronted the head referee on the field to demand an explanation for a flag he considered completely unjustified.

"I asked the ref about that during the game, and I thought that was a terrible call," Heyward revealed. "Calling the defense for holding when it's a downhill play. I literally went to the ref. I was like, 'What was wrong with that play? It was a double downhill.'"

According to Heyward, the official claimed the defender prevented an offensive lineman from climbing to the second level. Heyward quickly rejected that logic, pointing out that the play's design moved straight down the middle, making second-level obstruction irrelevant.

"That makes no sense because it was all downhill," Heyward said. "And I told the ref, I was like, 'Next time I see you, give me the reason. I don't know when I'm going to get it, but please watch this game. tell me if you were right in calling that because I think it was a terrible call in that moment.'"

Though Pittsburgh's defense held firm down the stretch to seal head coach Mike McCarthy's first win with the franchise, Heyward's postgame comments underscore his willingness to hold officials accountable when controversial penalties disrupt defensive momentum.

title: Did Carlota Ciganda deliver the Solheim Cup's greatest quote?
description: Carlota Ciganda, the most passionate player in the Solheim Cup, delivered what might be the event's greatest quote after Europe defeated the U.S.
fullText:
There's an admirable we're-all-here-to-grow-the-game attitude about the Solheim Cup. That's the goal, captains often say – repeatedly.

"We had already won at the start of the week with the bond that we had," vice captain Mel Reid during the winner's press conference.

That's lovely, of course, but it's not the kind of thing that generates headlines and draws attention.

More: 'I love beating the Americans': Europeans win 2026 Solheim Cup

To do that, players often need to show a little edge. And while many players of yesteryear had it in spades, few do amongst the current crop.

Despite the above quote, it's worth noting that Reid does have an edge, as does her good friend Carlota Ciganda, the most passionate player in the Solheim Cup who, on Sunday, delivered what might be the event's greatest quote.

Here it is ... @BrentleyGC's question to Carlota Ciganda and the answer that will live on in Solheim Cup lore ... 

"But today. I knew she had no chance. I was like, I want to kill you." 

Absolute theater. pic.twitter.com/VC0pagdP4p

After Jennifer Kupcho drained more than 100 feet of putts on the last two holes of Saturday's four-ball session against the player known as "Chiggy," the Americans moved into an 8-8 tie with the Europeans going into singles. Kupcho shouted "Vamos" after the 90-footer dropped on the 17th, a nod to Ciganda.

She had also "shushed" the crowd earlier in the afternoon after making birdie, though the U.S. still trailed in the match.

Later that night, when the singles lineup was revealed, it was Kupcho and Ciganda in the penultimate group.

The Spaniard came out firing, making birdies on Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 at Bernardus Golf to build a 4-up lead. The match ended on the par-5 16th, with Ciganda winning, 4 and 2.

Europe went on to reclaim the Solheim Cup, 15-13.

She was later asked in the winner's press conference by Golf Channel's Brentley Romine about her motivation coming into Sunday.

"I was really happy to see that I was playing against Kupcho," said Ciganda. "She's a fighter, I'm a fighter, and I told her, 'Look, great playing.' I mean, even yesterday, what she did was amazing on 17 and 18.

"But today, I knew she had no chance. I was like, 'I want to kill you.'"

Ciganda delivered the all-time quote in a cool, measured tone.

In two years – in 20 years – it won't be forgotten.

Beth Ann Nichols is a senior writer for Golfweek covering the LPGA and all things women's golf. Follow her on X/Twitter (@GolfweekNichols).

fullText:
The Oklahoma Sooners had a chance to win on the road, but the offense simply didn't show up. The Michigan Wolverines outmuscled them, and Oklahoma couldn't match the physicality. The two turnovers didn't help matters either in a one-touchdown game.

Now the Sooners are in a position with little room for error against one of the toughest schedules in college football. But don't count them out. After their loss to Ole Miss last year, the Sooners' College Football Playoff hopes were left for dead. Then they beat Tennessee and Alabama on the road and LSU and Missouri at home to save their season.

Each week, the ESPN Matchup Predictor updates their win probabilities for each team in college football. After Oklahoma's loss over Michigan, how has their season changed according to the computers?

Here's how ESPN Analytics projects the Oklahoma Sooners to fare in 2026.

Sooners Win Probability: 60.1% (Down from 73.4%)
